decks.title: Body Fluids and Circulation — Part 1: Blood, blood groups, clotting and lymph
goals: Describe the composition of plasma and the formed elements of blood
Explain ABO and Rh grouping and their importance in transfusion and pregnancy
Describe the clotting of blood and the formation and role of lymph

slides.heading: Body Fluids and Circulation
slides.body_md: Part 1 — blood, the most common body fluid in most higher organisms, and lymph.

visual.alt: Flow showing blood made of plasma and formed elements

slides.narration: Every living cell needs nutrients and oxygen and must get rid of wastes. Simple organisms like sponges and coelenterates circulate water from their surroundings. Most higher organisms, including us, use special fluids instead: blood and lymph. Blood is a special connective tissue made of a fluid matrix, plasma, and formed elements.

slides.heading: Plasma
slides.body_md: **Plasma** is a straw-coloured, viscous fluid forming nearly **55 percent** of blood. It is **90–92 percent water**; proteins make up **6–8 percent**.

rows: Mainly involved in the defence mechanisms of the body

visual.alt: Table of three major plasma proteins and their roles

slides.narration: Besides water and proteins, plasma carries small amounts of minerals such as sodium, calcium, magnesium, bicarbonate and chloride ions, along with glucose, amino acids and lipids that are in transit. Clotting factors are also present in an inactive form. Plasma without the clotting factors is called serum.

slides.heading: Formed elements
slides.body_md: **Erythrocytes, leucocytes and platelets** together form about **45 percent** of blood.

rows: Made in red bone marrow; no nucleus in most mammals; biconcave; haemoglobin; live about 120 days; destroyed in the spleen
Colourless, nucleated, generally short-lived; granulocytes and agranulocytes
Cell fragments from megakaryocytes in bone marrow; release clotting factors

visual.alt: Table comparing erythrocytes, leucocytes and platelets

slides.narration: Red blood cells are the most abundant cells. Their red pigment, haemoglobin, carries the respiratory gases; a healthy person has twelve to sixteen grams of it in every hundred millilitres of blood. The spleen, where old red cells are destroyed, is called the graveyard of red blood cells. A fall in the platelet count can lead to clotting disorders and heavy loss of blood.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: how much plasma?
slides.body_md: An adult has about 5000 mL of blood containing 15 g of haemoglobin per 100 mL. Using the textbook shares, how much is plasma, how much is formed elements, and how much haemoglobin is carried?
bullets: Plasma: $5000 \times \dfrac{55}{100} = 2750$ mL.
Formed elements: $5000 \times \dfrac{45}{100} = 2250$ mL.
Haemoglobin: $\dfrac{5000}{100} \times 15 = 750$ g.

visual.alt: Worked table: 2750 mL plasma, 2250 mL formed elements, 750 g haemoglobin

slides.narration: Fifty five percent of five thousand millilitres is two thousand seven hundred and fifty millilitres of plasma, leaving two thousand two hundred and fifty for the cells. Fifty lots of fifteen grams give seven hundred and fifty grams of haemoglobin. Real blood volumes vary with body size.

slides.heading: Quick check: red blood cells
slides.body_md: Answer the question about mature human red blood cells.
slides.narration: Quick check. What do most mammalian red cells lose as they mature?

slides.heading: Leucocytes
slides.body_md: **Granulocytes:** neutrophils, eosinophils and basophils. **Agranulocytes:** lymphocytes and monocytes.

rows: B and T lymphocytes: immune responses
Resist infections; linked with allergic reactions
Secrete histamine, serotonin and heparin; inflammatory reactions

visual.alt: Table of five kinds of leucocytes with their shares and roles

slides.narration: Neutrophils are the most abundant white cells and basophils the least. Neutrophils and monocytes are phagocytic cells that destroy foreign organisms. Basophils release histamine, serotonin and heparin in inflammatory reactions. Eosinophils resist infections and are associated with allergies. Lymphocytes, of the B and T kinds, carry out immune responses.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: reading a WBC count
slides.body_md: A blood report gives a total leucocyte count of 7000 per cubic millimetre, with neutrophils 62 percent and lymphocytes 22 percent. Find the number of each per cubic millimetre and say whether the total is normal.
bullets: Neutrophils: $7000 \times \dfrac{62}{100} = 4340$.
Lymphocytes: $7000 \times \dfrac{22}{100} = 1540$.
The total lies inside the usual range of 6,000 to 8,000 per cubic millimetre.

visual.alt: Worked table: 4340 neutrophils and 1540 lymphocytes per cubic millimetre

slides.narration: Multiply the total count by each share. Sixty two percent of seven thousand is four thousand three hundred and forty neutrophils, and twenty two percent is one thousand five hundred and forty lymphocytes. Both shares, and the total, are within the normal ranges.

slides.heading: ABO blood groups
slides.body_md: Grouping is based on the **presence or absence of two surface antigens, A and B**, on red cells. Plasma carries **natural antibodies** against the antigen that is absent.

visual.alt: Table of ABO blood groups with antigens, antibodies and compatible donor groups

slides.narration: Before a transfusion, donor blood must be matched with the recipient, or the recipient’s antibodies will attack the donated red cells and cause clumping. Group O has neither antigen, so its cells can be given to anyone: a universal donor. Group AB has no antibodies and can receive from all groups: a universal recipient.

slides.heading: Quick check: matching blood
slides.body_md: Choose the safe donors for the patient described.
slides.narration: Quick check. Which donor antigens would the patient’s antibodies attack?

slides.heading: Rh grouping and pregnancy
slides.body_md: Nearly **80 percent** of humans carry the **Rh antigen** (Rh positive). An **Rh-negative** person exposed to Rh-positive blood forms **anti-Rh antibodies**.

nodes.label: At delivery a little foetal blood enters the mother
Next Rh-positive foetus: antibodies destroy its red cells

visual.alt: Flow showing how Rh incompatibility leads to erythroblastosis foetalis

slides.narration: In the first pregnancy the placenta keeps the two bloods apart. At delivery the mother may be exposed to a small amount of the baby’s Rh positive blood and start making antibodies. In a later pregnancy these can leak into the foetus, destroying its red cells and causing severe anaemia and jaundice. Giving anti Rh antibodies to the mother right after the first delivery prevents this.

slides.heading: Coagulation of blood
slides.body_md: A **clot** is mainly a network of **fibrin** threads in which dead and damaged formed elements are trapped. It prevents excessive loss of blood.

nodes.label: Injury: platelets and damaged tissue release factors
Cascade of plasma factors forms thrombokinase
Clot: fibrin network traps formed elements

visual.alt: Flow of the clotting cascade from injury through thrombokinase, thrombin and fibrin to a clot

slides.narration: An injury makes platelets release certain factors, and damaged tissues release others. These start a cascade of linked enzyme reactions that forms thrombokinase. Thrombokinase helps convert inactive prothrombin into the enzyme thrombin, and thrombin turns soluble fibrinogen into fibrin threads. Calcium ions play a very important role in clotting.

slides.heading: Quick check: Rh factor
slides.body_md: Judge the assertion and the reason about the Rh factor.
slides.narration: Quick check. Are anti Rh antibodies present from birth, or made after exposure?

slides.heading: Tissue fluid and lymph
slides.body_md: As blood passes through capillaries, water and small water-soluble substances move into the spaces between cells, leaving larger proteins and most formed elements behind. This is **interstitial (tissue) fluid**. The **lymphatic system** collects it and drains it back into major veins; the fluid inside it is **lymph**.

rows: Exchange of nutrients and gases with cells; carries nutrients and hormones; fats absorbed through lacteals in intestinal villi

visual.alt: Table of the features and roles of lymph

slides.narration: Tissue fluid is the go between for blood and body cells: nutrients and gases are exchanged through it. Lymph returns this fluid to the blood, carries lymphocytes for immunity, and transports absorbed fats from the lacteals of the intestinal villi.

slides.heading: Quick check: lymph
slides.body_md: How does lymph differ from blood?
slides.narration: Quick check. What stays behind in the capillaries when tissue fluid forms?

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Plasma about 55 percent (fibrinogen, globulins, albumins); formed elements about 45 percent.
RBCs: 5–5.5 million per cubic mm, haemoglobin 12–16 g per 100 mL, life 120 days; WBCs: 6000–8000; platelets: 1.5–3.5 lakh.
ABO groups depend on antigens A and B; O universal donor, AB universal recipient.
Rh incompatibility can cause erythroblastosis foetalis; prevented by anti-Rh antibodies after the first delivery.
Clotting: thrombokinase, prothrombin to thrombin, fibrinogen to fibrin; calcium ions needed.
Lymph returns tissue fluid to veins, carries lymphocytes and absorbed fats.

rows: Fluid matrix with proteins and clotting factors

visual.alt: Summary table of plasma, serum and lymph

slides.narration: To recap: blood is plasma plus formed elements. Red cells carry gases, white cells defend, and platelets help clotting. Blood groups decide who can donate to whom, and Rh incompatibility matters in pregnancy. Lymph returns tissue fluid to the blood.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Learn the **three plasma proteins** with one role each.
Draw the **ABO table** from antigens and antibodies; do not memorise it blindly.
Write the clotting sequence in order: **thrombokinase → thrombin → fibrin**, with **calcium ions**.
Do not confuse **serum** with **plasma**, or **universal donor** with **universal recipient**.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Know the three plasma proteins and their roles. Build the blood group table from antigens and antibodies. Write the clotting steps in the right order and mention calcium ions. And keep serum and plasma, and donor and recipient, clearly apart.

decks.title: Body Fluids and Circulation — Part 2: The heart, cardiac cycle, ECG, double circulation and disorders
goals: Compare open and closed circulation and the hearts of vertebrates
Describe the human heart, its conducting system, the cardiac cycle and the ECG
Explain double circulation and the regulation of cardiac activity
Describe hypertension, coronary artery disease, angina and heart failure

slides.heading: The circulatory system
slides.body_md: Part 2 — how the heart pumps blood round the body, and what can go wrong.

visual.alt: Flow of blood from the heart through arteries, capillaries and veins back to the heart

slides.narration: The human circulatory system, also called the blood vascular system, has a muscular chambered heart, a network of closed branching blood vessels, and blood, the fluid that circulates. First we compare circulatory patterns in animals, then look closely at the human heart.

slides.heading: Circulatory pathways
slides.body_md: **Open** system: blood pumped by the heart passes through large vessels into open spaces called **sinuses** (arthropods, molluscs). **Closed** system: blood always stays inside vessels (annelids, chordates), so flow can be regulated more precisely.

rows: Single: heart pumps deoxygenated blood to the gills
Incomplete double: blood mixes in the single ventricle

visual.alt: Table of heart chambers and circulation in vertebrate groups

slides.narration: All vertebrates have a muscular chambered heart. In fishes the heart pumps out deoxygenated blood, which is oxygenated in the gills. In amphibians and most reptiles, oxygenated and deoxygenated blood mix in one ventricle. Crocodiles, birds and mammals keep the two kinds of blood completely apart.

slides.heading: The human heart
slides.body_md: Mesodermal in origin; in the thoracic cavity between the lungs, slightly tilted to the left; about the size of a clenched fist; enclosed in the double-walled **pericardium** with pericardial fluid.

slides.narration: The two upper chambers, the atria, are small; the two lower ventricles are larger and have much thicker walls. A thin interatrial septum and a thick interventricular septum separate the left and right sides. The tricuspid valve guards the right atrioventricular opening, the bicuspid or mitral valve the left, and semilunar valves guard the pulmonary artery and aorta, so blood flows one way only.

slides.heading: Nodal tissue: the conducting system
slides.body_md: Specialised cardiac musculature, the **nodal tissue**, is **autoexcitable**: it generates action potentials without any external stimulus. The **SAN** produces the most, about **70–75 per minute**, so it is the **pacemaker**.

nodes.label: Sino-atrial node (upper right corner of right atrium)
Atrio-ventricular node (lower left corner of right atrium)
AV bundle, right and left bundles

visual.alt: Flow of the cardiac impulse from the SA node through the AV node and bundle of His to the Purkinje fibres

slides.narration: The atrio ventricular bundle runs from the atrio ventricular node through the septum and divides into right and left bundles, which give rise to minute Purkinje fibres throughout the ventricles. The bundles and Purkinje fibres together are called the bundle of His. Because the heartbeat starts in its own muscle, the heart is called myogenic.

slides.heading: Quick check: pacemaker
slides.body_md: Which part of the heart sets its pace?
slides.narration: Quick check. Which node generates the most action potentials per minute?

slides.heading: The cardiac cycle
slides.body_md: The sequence of events in the heart that repeats with every beat: **systole** (contraction) and **diastole** (relaxation) of both atria and ventricles.

rows: All chambers relaxed; tricuspid and bicuspid valves open; semilunar valves closed; blood flows from veins through atria into ventricles
SAN fires; both atria contract, adding about 30 percent more blood to the ventricles
Impulse spreads by AVN and bundle of His; ventricles contract, atria relax; AV valves close (lub); semilunar valves open
Ventricles relax; semilunar valves close (dub); AV valves reopen and the cycle restarts

visual.alt: Table of the four stages of the cardiac cycle

slides.narration: Ventricular contraction raises the pressure, which shuts the tricuspid and bicuspid valves as blood tries to flow back. That closure makes the first sound, lub. When the ventricles relax, the semilunar valves shut to stop backflow, giving the second sound, dub. These sounds are clinically important.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: cycle length and cardiac output
slides.body_md: A healthy adult’s heart beats 72 times a minute and each ventricle pumps about 70 mL per beat (the stroke volume). How long is one cardiac cycle, and what is the cardiac output?
bullets: Cycle length: $\dfrac{60}{72} \approx 0.833$ s, usually quoted as about 0.8 s.
Cardiac output is stroke volume times heart rate: $70 \times 72 = 5040$ mL per minute.
That is about 5 litres per minute, the textbook average. An athlete’s output can be much higher.

visual.alt: Worked table: cycle about 0.8 second, cardiac output 5040 millilitres per minute

slides.narration: Sixty seconds shared among seventy two beats gives about zero point eight of a second per cycle. Seventy millilitres per beat times seventy two beats gives five thousand and forty millilitres, roughly five litres every minute from each ventricle.

slides.heading: The electrocardiogram (ECG)
slides.body_md: An **ECG** is a graphical record of the electrical activity of the heart during a cardiac cycle. For a standard ECG, leads are attached to each wrist and to the left ankle.

visual.alt: Standard ECG trace showing P wave, QRS complex and T wave, with one R to R interval marked as one cardiac cycle

slides.narration: The P wave shows excitation, or depolarisation, of the atria, which makes them contract. The QRS complex shows depolarisation of the ventricles; their contraction starts shortly after Q. The T wave shows the ventricles returning to the normal state, and its end marks the end of systole. Deviations from the normal shape point to heart disease.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: heart rate from an ECG
slides.body_md: An ECG strip recorded for 15 seconds shows 18 QRS complexes. What is the heart rate, and how long is each cardiac cycle?
bullets: Rate: $\dfrac{18 \times 60}{15} = 72$ beats per minute.
Cycle: $\dfrac{15}{18} \approx 0.83$ s, about 0.8 s.
Each QRS complex marks one ventricular contraction, so counting them gives the heart rate.

visual.alt: Worked table: 18 QRS complexes in 15 seconds give 72 beats per minute

slides.narration: Eighteen beats in a quarter of a minute means four times eighteen, seventy two beats a minute. Doctors count QRS complexes over a fixed time in exactly this way.

slides.heading: Quick check: ECG waves
slides.body_md: What does the P wave of an ECG represent?
slides.narration: Quick check. Which chambers are excited first?

slides.heading: Double circulation
slides.body_md: **Pulmonary circulation:** right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary veins → left atrium. **Systemic circulation:** left ventricle → aorta → arteries, arterioles, capillaries → tissues → venules, veins, venae cavae → right atrium.

slides.narration: Blood passes through the heart twice in one full circuit, so oxygenated and deoxygenated blood never mix. The systemic circuit supplies tissues with nutrients and oxygen and removes carbon dioxide and other harmful substances. The hepatic portal vein takes blood from the intestine to the liver before it joins the systemic circulation, and a coronary system serves the heart muscle itself.

notes.title: Body Fluids and Circulation — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Blood, blood groups, coagulation and lymph
sections.body_md:
Simple organisms such as sponges and coelenterates circulate water from their surroundings through their body cavities. Most higher organisms use special body fluids: **blood** and **lymph**.

**Blood** is a special connective tissue made of a fluid matrix, **plasma**, and **formed elements**.

**Plasma** (about **55 percent** of blood) is a straw-coloured, viscous fluid: **90–92 percent water** and **6–8 percent proteins**. **Fibrinogen** is needed for clotting, **globulins** are mainly involved in defence, and **albumins** help in osmotic balance. Plasma also carries small amounts of minerals (sodium, calcium, magnesium, bicarbonate and chloride ions), glucose, amino acids and lipids in transit, and the **clotting factors** in an inactive form. Plasma without clotting factors is **serum**.

**Formed elements** (about **45 percent**):
- **Erythrocytes (RBCs)** are the most abundant cells: **5–5.5 million per cubic millimetre** in a healthy adult man. In adults they are formed in the **red bone marrow**. Most mammalian RBCs have **no nucleus** and are **biconcave**. They contain the iron-containing red pigment **haemoglobin**, **12–16 g per 100 mL** of blood, which transports respiratory gases. They live about **120 days** and are destroyed in the **spleen** (the graveyard of RBCs).
- **Leucocytes (WBCs)** are colourless (no haemoglobin), nucleated, relatively fewer (**6000–8000 per cubic millimetre**) and generally short-lived. **Granulocytes**: neutrophils (most abundant, **60–65 percent**, phagocytic), eosinophils (**2–3 percent**, resist infections, associated with allergic reactions) and basophils (least, **0.5–1 percent**, secrete histamine, serotonin and heparin; inflammatory reactions). **Agranulocytes**: lymphocytes (**20–25 percent**, B and T forms, immune responses) and monocytes (**6–8 percent**, phagocytic).
- **Platelets (thrombocytes)** are cell fragments produced from **megakaryocytes** in the bone marrow, **1.5–3.5 lakh per cubic millimetre**. They release substances involved in coagulation; a fall in their number can cause clotting disorders and excessive loss of blood.

(Counts are typical textbook values; laboratories quote slightly different normal ranges.)

**ABO grouping** depends on the presence or absence of **antigens A and B** on the RBC surface; plasma contains **natural antibodies** against the antigen that is absent. Group A (antigen A, anti-B) receives from A and O; group B (antigen B, anti-A) from B and O; group AB (both antigens, no antibodies) from all groups — the **universal recipient**; group O (no antigens, both antibodies) only from O but can donate to all — the **universal donor**. Donor blood must be matched before transfusion to avoid clumping (destruction) of RBCs.

**Rh grouping:** the Rh antigen, similar to one in Rhesus monkeys, is present on the RBCs of nearly **80 percent** of humans (Rh positive). An **Rh-negative** person exposed to Rh-positive blood forms specific antibodies against the Rh antigen. In pregnancy, if the mother is Rh negative and the foetus Rh positive, the placenta keeps the bloods apart in the first pregnancy, but at the first delivery the mother may be exposed to a small amount of foetal blood and begins to make anti-Rh antibodies. In later pregnancies these can leak into the foetal blood and destroy its RBCs, causing severe anaemia and jaundice — **erythroblastosis foetalis**. It is avoided by giving **anti-Rh antibodies** to the mother immediately after the first delivery.

**Coagulation:** a clot (coagulum) is a network of **fibrin** threads trapping dead and damaged formed elements. Fibrin forms from inactive **fibrinogen** by the enzyme **thrombin**; thrombin forms from inactive **prothrombin**, a reaction that needs the enzyme complex **thrombokinase**. Thrombokinase forms by a **cascade** of linked enzymic reactions involving factors present in plasma in an inactive state. An injury stimulates **platelets** to release factors that start the cascade; factors released by damaged **tissues** can also start it. **Calcium ions** play a very important role.

**Lymph:** as blood passes through capillaries, water and small water-soluble substances move into the spaces between cells, leaving larger proteins and most formed elements in the vessels. This **interstitial (tissue) fluid** has the same mineral distribution as plasma; nutrients and gases are exchanged between blood and cells through it. The **lymphatic system** collects it and drains it back into major veins; the fluid inside is **lymph** — colourless, with specialised **lymphocytes** for immune responses. Lymph carries nutrients and hormones, and **fats are absorbed through lymph in the lacteals** of the intestinal villi.

sections.heading: 2. Circulatory pathways, the human heart and the cardiac cycle
sections.body_md:
**Circulatory pathways.** In an **open** system (arthropods, molluscs) blood pumped by the heart passes through large vessels into open spaces or body cavities called **sinuses**. In a **closed** system (annelids, chordates) blood is always pumped through a closed network of vessels, which allows more precise regulation of flow. All vertebrates have a muscular, chambered heart: **fishes 2 chambers** (an atrium and a ventricle), **amphibians and reptiles 3** (two atria, one ventricle; crocodiles are the exception), and **crocodiles, birds and mammals 4**. In fishes the heart pumps out deoxygenated blood, which is oxygenated in the gills and supplied to the body (**single circulation**). In amphibians and reptiles the left atrium receives oxygenated blood (from gills, lungs or skin) and the right atrium deoxygenated blood, and they mix in the single ventricle (**incomplete double circulation**). Birds and mammals have two separate pathways (**double circulation**).

**The human heart** is mesodermal in origin, lies in the thoracic cavity between the two lungs, slightly tilted to the left, and is about the size of a clenched fist. It is protected by a double-walled membranous bag, the **pericardium**, enclosing **pericardial fluid**. It has two small upper **atria** and two larger lower **ventricles**. A thin **interatrial septum** separates the atria and a thick **interventricular septum** the ventricles; a thick fibrous **atrio-ventricular septum** separates the atrium and ventricle of each side, with an opening guarded by the **tricuspid valve** (right) or the **bicuspid (mitral) valve** (left). The openings of the right and left ventricles into the **pulmonary artery** and **aorta** have **semilunar valves**. Valves allow blood to flow in one direction only. The heart is made of cardiac muscle; the ventricle walls are much thicker than those of the atria.

**Nodal tissue** is specialised cardiac musculature. The **sino-atrial node (SAN)** lies in the right upper corner of the right atrium; the **atrio-ventricular node (AVN)** in the lower left corner of the right atrium, close to the atrio-ventricular septum. The **atrio-ventricular bundle** runs from the AVN through the septum to the top of the interventricular septum and divides into right and left bundles, which give rise to minute **Purkinje fibres** throughout the ventricular muscle; the bundles and Purkinje fibres together form the **bundle of His**. Nodal muscle is **autoexcitable**. The SAN generates the most action potentials, **70–75 per minute**, so it is the **pacemaker**; the normal heart rate is **72 beats per minute**.

**Cardiac cycle.** In **joint diastole** all four chambers are relaxed; the tricuspid and bicuspid valves are open and the semilunar valves closed, and blood flows from the pulmonary veins and venae cavae through the atria into the ventricles. The SAN fires and both atria contract (**atrial systole**), increasing the flow into the ventricles by about **30 percent**. The impulse passes through the AVN and AV bundle, and the bundle of His spreads it through the ventricles, which contract (**ventricular systole**) while the atria relax. Rising ventricular pressure **closes the tricuspid and bicuspid valves** (attempted backflow) and then **forces open the semilunar valves**, so blood enters the pulmonary artery and aorta. The ventricles then relax (**ventricular diastole**); the **semilunar valves close**, and as the pressure falls further the AV valves are pushed open by blood in the atria. All chambers are again in joint diastole until the SAN fires again.

With **72 beats per minute**, one cardiac cycle lasts about **0.8 s**. Each ventricle pumps about **70 mL** per cycle (**stroke volume**). **Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate**, about **5000 mL (5 L) per minute** in a healthy person; an athlete’s cardiac output can be much higher. The first heart sound, **lub**, comes from closure of the tricuspid and bicuspid valves; the second, **dub**, from closure of the semilunar valves.

**Electrocardiogram (ECG):** a graph of the electrical activity of the heart during a cardiac cycle. For a standard ECG, leads are attached to each wrist and to the left ankle. The **P wave** is depolarisation of the atria (leading to their contraction); the **QRS complex** is depolarisation of the ventricles, which starts ventricular contraction shortly after Q and marks the beginning of systole; the **T wave** is the return of the ventricles to the normal state (repolarisation), and its end marks the end of systole. Counting QRS complexes in a given time gives the heart rate; deviations from the normal shape indicate abnormality or disease.

sections.heading: 3. Double circulation and regulation of cardiac activity
sections.body_md:
Blood pumped by the **right ventricle** enters the **pulmonary artery** and is carried to the lungs; oxygenated blood returns by the **pulmonary veins** to the **left atrium** — the **pulmonary circulation**. Blood pumped by the **left ventricle** enters the **aorta** and is carried by arteries, arterioles and capillaries to the tissues; deoxygenated blood is collected by venules, veins and the **venae cavae** and emptied into the **right atrium** — the **systemic circulation**. The systemic circulation supplies nutrients, oxygen and other essential substances to the tissues and takes carbon dioxide and other harmful substances away for elimination. This passage of blood twice through the heart in one complete circuit is **double circulation**.

A unique vascular connection, the **hepatic portal system**, links the digestive tract and the liver: the **hepatic portal vein** carries blood from the intestine to the liver before it is delivered to the systemic circulation. A special **coronary system** of blood vessels serves only the circulation of blood to and from the cardiac muscle.

**Regulation.** Normal heart activity is regulated intrinsically, that is auto-regulated by the nodal tissue, so the heart is called **myogenic**. A special neural centre in the **medulla oblongata** can moderate cardiac function through the **autonomic nervous system**. **Sympathetic** nerves increase the rate of the heartbeat and the strength of ventricular contraction, and thereby the cardiac output. **Parasympathetic** signals decrease the heart rate and the speed of conduction of the action potential, and thereby the cardiac output. **Adrenal medullary hormones** can also increase the cardiac output.

Left ventricle → aorta → tissues → venae cavae → right atrium.
Hepatic portal vein carrying blood from the intestine to the liver before it enters the systemic circulation.
A heart whose beat starts in its own specialised muscle (nodal tissue).

sections.heading: 4. Disorders of the circulatory system
sections.body_md:
- **High blood pressure (hypertension):** blood pressure higher than normal (**120/80 mm Hg**; 120 is the systolic, or pumping, pressure and 80 the diastolic, or resting, pressure). If repeated checks show **140/90 mm Hg or higher**, it is hypertension. It leads to heart disease and also affects vital organs such as the **brain and kidneys**.
- **Coronary artery disease (CAD)**, often called **atherosclerosis**, affects the vessels supplying blood to the heart muscle. Deposits of **calcium, fat, cholesterol and fibrous tissue** make the lumen of the arteries narrower.
- **Angina (angina pectoris):** a symptom of **acute chest pain** when not enough oxygen reaches the heart muscle. It can occur in men and women of any age but is more common among the middle-aged and elderly, and arises from conditions that affect blood flow.
- **Heart failure:** the heart is not pumping blood effectively enough to meet the needs of the body. It is sometimes called **congestive heart failure** because congestion of the lungs is one of its main symptoms. It is **not the same as cardiac arrest** (the heart stops beating) or a **heart attack** (heart muscle is suddenly damaged by an inadequate blood supply).

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing that group AB is the universal donor (it is the universal recipient; O is the universal donor).
- Saying anti-Rh antibodies are present from birth (they form only after exposure to Rh-positive blood).
- Placing the semilunar valves between the atria and ventricles (they guard the pulmonary artery and aorta).
- Calling the AVN the pacemaker (the SAN is the pacemaker).
- Saying the T wave shows atrial contraction (it is ventricular repolarisation).
- Treating heart failure, heart attack and cardiac arrest as the same.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: a plasma protein, a WBC type, a valve, an ECG wave, a blood group fact.
- 2–3-mark answers: plasma composition; ABO and Rh; clotting steps; nodal tissue; cardiac cycle; double circulation; regulation; hypertension and CAD.
- 5-mark answers: composition of blood; the heart and the cardiac cycle with ECG; double circulation and regulation; disorders.
- Numericals: cardiac output, cycle length, heart rate from an ECG, shares of blood components — always show the formula and units.

questions.stem_md: A test tube of blood treated to stop clotting is left standing. A pale straw-coloured fluid forming a little more than half of the column collects at the top. This fluid is

options.text_md: lymph, the fluid of the lymphatic vessels
the formed elements, about 45 percent of blood
haemoglobin released from burst red cells
plasma, about 55 percent of blood

questions.solution_md: The fluid matrix of blood is plasma, a straw-coloured viscous fluid forming about 55 percent of blood — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A patient’s liver makes too little of one plasma protein, and even a small cut on her finger keeps oozing blood for a long time. Which protein is most likely to be deficient?

options.text_md: Albumin
Globulin
Haemoglobin
Fibrinogen

questions.solution_md: Fibrinogen is needed for clotting; albumins help osmotic balance and globulins defence, while haemoglobin is in red cells, not plasma — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Which statement about the mature red blood cells of most mammals, including humans, is correct?

options.text_md: They have a large nucleus and are spherical.
They have no nucleus and are biconcave in shape.
They are made in the spleen and destroyed in the bone marrow.
They live for about 12 days.

questions.solution_md: Most mammalian RBCs are devoid of a nucleus and biconcave; they are formed in red bone marrow, live about 120 days and are destroyed in the spleen — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A laboratory technician identifies and tallies 200 white blood cells in a stained smear from a healthy adult. Which type will she most probably tally most often?

options.text_md: Neutrophils
Basophils
Monocytes
Eosinophils

questions.solution_md: Neutrophils are the most abundant leucocytes, 60–65 percent; basophils are the least, 0.5–1 percent — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A boy with hay fever, who sneezes every spring when grasses flower, shows a raised count of one kind of granulocyte. Which leucocyte is it most likely to be?

options.text_md: Lymphocytes
Monocytes
Erythrocytes
Eosinophils

questions.solution_md: Eosinophils (2–3 percent of WBCs) resist infections and are associated with allergic reactions; lymphocytes and monocytes are agranulocytes — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A patient of blood group B needs a transfusion of red cells. Donors of groups A, B, AB and O are available. Which donors are compatible?

options.text_md: Group B only
Groups A, B and AB
Groups B and O only
All four groups

questions.solution_md: Group B plasma has anti-A antibodies, so red cells carrying antigen A (groups A and AB) would be attacked. Groups B and O carry no antigen A — option (c).

questions.stem_md: An Rh-negative woman had an Rh-positive first baby and received no treatment after delivery. She is now carrying a second Rh-positive foetus. What is the main risk?

options.text_md: The foetus will make antibodies that destroy the mother’s red cells during the pregnancy.
There is no risk, because Rh antigens and antibodies can never cross the placenta.
Her own blood group will change to Rh positive after the second delivery.
Her anti-Rh antibodies may enter the foetal blood and destroy its red cells (erythroblastosis foetalis).

questions.solution_md: She was sensitised at the first delivery and now has anti-Rh antibodies, which can leak into the Rh-positive foetus and destroy its RBCs, causing severe anaemia and jaundice — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Blood banks add a citrate salt, which binds calcium ions, to the bags in which donated blood is collected. Why?

options.text_md: Calcium ions destroy red blood cells during storage.
Citrate supplies energy to the platelets so that they multiply.
Calcium ions turn fibrin back into fibrinogen.
Calcium ions are needed for coagulation, so removing them keeps the blood from clotting.

questions.solution_md: Calcium ions play a very important role in the clotting cascade; binding them prevents coagulation of stored blood — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Compared with blood, lymph lacks

options.text_md: water and the dissolved minerals of plasma
lymphocytes and all other white blood cells
red blood cells and the larger plasma proteins
all dissolved nutrients, such as glucose

questions.solution_md: Tissue fluid forms as water and small water-soluble substances leave the capillaries, leaving larger proteins and most formed elements behind; lymph is colourless but contains lymphocytes — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Platelets are cell fragments produced from large cells of the bone marrow called ______.
questions.solution_md: Megakaryocytes.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A person of blood group O is a universal recipient because his plasma has no anti-A or anti-B antibodies.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. Group O plasma has both anti-A and anti-B; group O is the universal donor because its red cells carry no A or B antigen. Group AB, with no antibodies, is the universal recipient.

questions.stem_md: Match each leucocyte (column I) with its main role (column II).

options.text_md: Neutrophils
Basophils
Eosinophils
Lymphocytes

match_right.text_md: B and T cells responsible for immune responses
Most abundant phagocytes, destroying foreign organisms
Resist infections; linked with allergic reactions

questions.solution_md: Neutrophils are the main phagocytes; basophils release histamine, serotonin and heparin; eosinophils are linked with allergies; lymphocytes (B and T) carry out immune responses.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A healthy adult man has about 5 to 5.5 million red blood cells per cubic millimetre of blood.

**Reason (R):** In adults, red blood cells are formed in the red bone marrow.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true, but the site of formation does not explain the count — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** An Rh-negative person who receives Rh-positive blood can produce antibodies against the Rh antigen.

**Reason (R):** Every Rh-negative person carries anti-Rh antibodies in the plasma from birth.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true; R is false, because anti-Rh antibodies form only after exposure to Rh-positive blood — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A large adult has about 6000 mL of blood. If plasma makes up 55 percent of blood, what volume of plasma, in mL, does this person have?
A boy’s total leucocyte count is 8000 per cubic millimetre, of which 25 percent are lymphocytes. How many lymphocytes are there per cubic millimetre?
questions.solution_md: $8000 \times \dfrac{25}{100} = 2000$ lymphocytes per cubic millimetre.

questions.stem_md: A school blood-donation camp tests 40 students. If the textbook figure of nearly 80 percent Rh-positive people holds, about how many students are expected to be Rh positive?
questions.solution_md: $40 \times \dfrac{80}{100} = 32$ students.

questions.stem_md: List the main constituents of plasma and state the role of each of its three major proteins.

answer.model_answer_md: Plasma is **90–92 percent water** with **6–8 percent proteins**, plus minerals, glucose, amino acids, lipids and inactive clotting factors. **Fibrinogen** is needed for clotting, **globulins** are mainly involved in defence, and **albumins** help maintain osmotic balance.

questions.solution_md: Constituents and protein roles.

questions.stem_md: How is tissue fluid formed, and what are two functions of lymph?

answer.model_answer_md: As blood flows through capillaries, **water and small water-soluble substances** move into the spaces between cells, leaving larger proteins and most formed elements behind: this is **tissue fluid**. Lymph returns it to major veins, carries **lymphocytes** for immunity, and transports **absorbed fats** from the lacteals.

questions.solution_md: Formation and two functions.

questions.stem_md: Using antigens and antibodies, explain why a person of group A must not receive red cells from a group B donor, whereas a person of group AB can safely receive them.

answer.model_answer_md:
Group B red cells carry **antigen B**. A group A person has **anti-B antibodies** in the plasma, which would react with the donated cells and cause them to **clump and be destroyed**, a dangerous transfusion reaction.

A group AB person has **both antigens A and B** on his own cells and therefore **no anti-A or anti-B antibodies**, so nothing attacks the donated group B cells. This is why AB is called the **universal recipient**.

questions.stem_md: Describe the structure of the human heart, including its chambers, septa, valves and the nodal tissue that controls its beat.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Position and covering.** The heart, mesodermal in origin, lies in the thoracic cavity between the lungs, slightly tilted to the left, and is about the size of a clenched fist. It is enclosed in the double-walled pericardium containing pericardial fluid.

**Chambers and septa.** It has two small upper atria and two larger lower ventricles with much thicker walls. A thin interatrial septum separates the atria and a thick interventricular septum the ventricles. A thick fibrous atrio-ventricular septum separates the atrium and ventricle of each side.

**Valves.** The right atrioventricular opening is guarded by the tricuspid valve and the left by the bicuspid or mitral valve. Semilunar valves guard the openings of the right ventricle into the pulmonary artery and of the left ventricle into the aorta. Valves let blood flow one way only.

**Nodal tissue.** The sino-atrial node lies in the right upper corner of the right atrium and the atrio-ventricular node in the lower left corner of the right atrium. The AV bundle runs from the AVN through the septum and divides into right and left bundles, which give rise to Purkinje fibres in the ventricle walls; together these form the bundle of His. Nodal muscle is autoexcitable; the SAN produces the most action potentials, 70–75 per minute, and is the pacemaker, so the heart is myogenic.

**Events.** In joint diastole all chambers are relaxed, the tricuspid and bicuspid valves are open and the semilunar valves closed, and blood flows from the venae cavae and pulmonary veins through the atria into the ventricles. The impulse reaches the ventricles through the AVN, AV bundle and bundle of His, and the ventricles contract while the atria relax. Rising pressure closes the AV valves and then forces open the semilunar valves, so blood enters the pulmonary artery and aorta. When the ventricles relax the semilunar valves close; the AV valves then open and the cycle restarts.

**Sounds.** Lub is produced by closure of the tricuspid and bicuspid valves; dub by closure of the semilunar valves.

**Calculations.** One cycle lasts $\dfrac{60}{72} \approx 0.833$ s, about 0.8 s. Cardiac output is stroke volume times heart rate: $70 \times 72 = 5040$ mL per minute, about 5 litres.

**ECG.** Each cycle shows a P wave (atrial depolarisation), a QRS complex (ventricular depolarisation, start of systole) and a T wave (ventricular repolarisation, end of systole).

questions.stem_md: Compare the circulation of a fish, a frog and a human, and explain why double circulation is considered more efficient. Describe also the hepatic portal and coronary systems of humans.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Fish.** The heart has two chambers, an atrium and a ventricle. It pumps out deoxygenated blood, which is oxygenated in the gills and supplied to the body; deoxygenated blood returns to the heart. Blood passes through the heart once per circuit: single circulation.

**Frog.** The heart has three chambers, two atria and one ventricle. The left atrium receives oxygenated blood from the lungs and skin and the right atrium deoxygenated blood from the body, but the two mix in the single ventricle, which pumps out mixed blood: incomplete double circulation.

**Human.** The four-chambered heart keeps the two sides apart. In the pulmonary circulation the right ventricle sends deoxygenated blood to the lungs, and the pulmonary veins return oxygenated blood to the left atrium. In the systemic circulation the left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood through the aorta to the tissues, and the venae cavae return deoxygenated blood to the right atrium.

**Why more efficient.** Oxygenated and deoxygenated blood never mix, so tissues receive fully oxygenated blood, and the left ventricle can pump it to the body under high pressure.

**Special systems.** The hepatic portal vein carries blood from the intestine to the liver before it enters the systemic circulation. The coronary system of vessels serves only the circulation of blood to and from the heart muscle.

answer.model_answer_md:
**First part.** The claim confuses heart failure with cardiac arrest. In cardiac arrest the heart stops beating, but in heart failure the heart is still beating; it simply does not pump blood effectively enough to meet the body’s needs. Congestion of the lungs is a main symptom, so it is also called congestive heart failure. A beating heart therefore does not rule it out.

**Second part.** Chest pain on exertion is typical of angina pectoris, which appears when not enough oxygen reaches the heart muscle. Its usual cause is coronary artery disease, or atherosclerosis, in which deposits of calcium, fat, cholesterol and fibrous tissue narrow the coronary arteries. This can be present even when blood pressure is normal, and a blocked artery can lead to a heart attack, in which heart muscle is suddenly damaged by inadequate blood supply.

**Blood pressure.** Normal pressure, about 120/80 mm Hg, is reassuring, and hypertension (repeated readings of 140/90 or higher) is itself a danger to the heart, brain and kidneys. But a normal reading does not exclude coronary disease.
